entries.consumer_display_name: Cochineal or carmines or carminic acid
entries.entry_title: Cochineal or carmines or carminic acid (120)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with animal or insect material. The target substance is separated from that material and then cleaned, refined or converted into a stable food-grade form.
entries.tile_summary: This red food colouring comes from insects — female cochineal insects, to be precise.
entries.expanded_summary: This red colouring has an unusual origin: female cochineal insects. Their pigment, carminic acid, is extracted from the dried insects and purified. It can also be prepared as carmine. Depending on local labelling rules, ingredient lists may say cochineal extract, carmine or colour (120).
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by extracting colour from dried female cochineal insects, then purifying it. Carmine is formed when that pigment is converted into a metal complex or colour lake.
entries.fact_1_copy: The colour is insect-derived, not plant-derived.
entries.fact_2_copy: The insect source can matter for vegan, vegetarian, religious or personal ingredient choices.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used to give foods a red to pink colour.
entries.evidence_copy: Some people can have allergic reactions to carmine or cochineal extract. For this reason, US food labels must identify these colour additives by name. If you have a confirmed allergy, check ingredient lists for 'carmine' or 'cochineal extract'.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: United States food regulator: Color additives questions and answers for consumers (current FDA page)

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Brilliant Blue FCF is a synthetic blue colour used for bright, stable blue shades and for colour blending.
entries.expanded_summary: Brilliant Blue FCF is a synthetic blue colour used for bright, stable blue shades and for colour blending.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by chemical synthesis and purified to a defined mixture of colouring substances.
entries.fact_1_copy: Produces a vivid blue and is often blended with other colours.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with an existing material — natural or manufactured — and deliberately transforms it using processes such as heating, roasting, oxidation, hydrolysis, neutralisation or other controlled treatment. The starting material can be materially changed in colour, structure or food-technology behaviour.
entries.tile_summary: Caramel II is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates.
entries.expanded_summary: Caramel II is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates. It is a colour ingredient, not simply the caramel made when sugar is browned in a kitchen.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by heated carbohydrates in the presence of sulphite compounds but not ammonium compounds, creating a complex mixture of brown colour compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Caustic sulphite caramel.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give foods and drinks brown to dark-brown colour.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Carotenes are yellow-orange pigments from the carotenoid family.
entries.expanded_summary: Carotenes are yellow-orange pigments from the carotenoid family. They occur naturally in many plants; commercial food colours can be extracted from plant sources or produced as defined carotene preparations.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Depending on the approved form, carotene preparations may be extracted from plant material or algae, or manufactured to provide defined carotene compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Beta-carotene is the pigment associated with the orange colour of carrots and many other fruits and vegetables.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for yellow to orange colouring.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Flavoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow colouring.
entries.expanded_summary: Flavoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow colouring. It belongs to the same broad natural pigment family as beta-carotene and lutein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: This carotenoid occurs in natural biological sources; commercial food-colour preparations may depend on the approved source and manufacturing specification.
entries.fact_1_copy: A xanthophyll carotenoid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for yellow colouring where permitted.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Beet red is a colour preparation based on betalain pigments from red beet.
entries.expanded_summary: Beet red is a colour preparation based on betalain pigments from red beet. Betanin is the principal red-violet pigment.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by extracting and concentrating colour from beetroot, with purification and drying as needed.
entries.fact_1_copy: The colour comes from red beet pigments.
entries.fact_2_copy: Provides red to purple-red colour.

entries.tile_summary: Elemental silver used as a metallic decorative colour where permitted.
entries.expanded_summary: Elemental silver used as a metallic decorative colour where permitted.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Refined silver is processed into very thin leaf, flakes or powder for food use.
entries.fact_1_copy: Primarily decorative, creating a metallic silver appearance.
entries.fact_2_copy: The additive is elemental silver prepared in a form suitable for decorative food use.

The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium sorbate is the calcium salt of sorbic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium sorbate is the calcium salt of sorbic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by reacting sorbic acid with a calcium source to form the preservative salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: One of the sorbate preservatives.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to inhibit moulds and yeasts where this salt form is suitable.

entries.tile_summary: Methylparaben is the methyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Methylparaben is the methyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying p-hydroxybenzoic acid with methanol and purifying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: A paraben preservative.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for antimicrobial preservation where permitted.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium sulphite is a potassium sulphite salt in the sulphite preservative family.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium sulphite is a potassium sulphite salt in the sulphite preservative family.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by neutralising sulphur dioxide with a potassium alkali.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for preservation and antioxidant effects.
entries.fact_2_copy: Chemically related to sulphur dioxide and other sulphites.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium nitrate is an inorganic nitrate salt.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium nitrate is an inorganic nitrate salt. In foods it is associated mainly with curing and preservation, particularly in meat processing.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially as a purified inorganic nitrate salt from mineral or chemical starting materials.
entries.fact_1_copy: Nitrite and nitrate chemistry is used to control microbes and help develop characteristic cured-meat colour and flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: This is a nitrate salt; nitrate can be converted to nitrite under some curing conditions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium acetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium acetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid. It provides acetate chemistry without adding acetic acid in exactly the same form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising acetic acid with a ammonium-containing base; diacetate forms also contain associated acetic acid.
entries.fact_1_copy: Chemically related to the acid found in vinegar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt and food, can help regulate acidity, preserve or influence flavour.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Carbon dioxide is the same gas produced by yeast fermentation and exhaled in breath.
entries.expanded_summary: Carbon dioxide is the same gas produced by yeast fermentation and exhaled in breath. In food it is used for carbonation, packaging atmospheres and processing.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced and purified from fermentation, ammonia manufacture or other industrial gas streams, then compressed or liquefied to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: The bubbles in carbonated drinks are dissolved carbon dioxide.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can also help displace oxygen in packaging or create protective atmospheres.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium ascorbate is the potassium salt of ascorbic acid — vitamin C.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium ascorbate is the potassium salt of ascorbic acid — vitamin C. It provides ascorbate antioxidant chemistry in a salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified ascorbic acid with a potassium-containing base; the ascorbic acid itself is usually produced from glucose by industrial fermentation/chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: It is chemically related to vitamin C and supplies ascorbate.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for antioxidant, colour-protection or processing effects.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Delta-tocopherol is one of the naturally occurring tocopherols in the vitamin E family.
entries.expanded_summary: Delta-tocopherol is one of the naturally occurring tocopherols in the vitamin E family. It is fat-soluble and can help slow oxidation.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade material is commonly isolated and purified from vegetable-oil fractions rich in tocopherols.
entries.fact_1_copy: Found naturally in vegetable oils and other plant foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antioxidant in fat-containing foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: tert-Butylhydroquinone (TBHQ) is a synthetic phenolic antioxidant particularly effective in fats and oils.
entries.expanded_summary: tert-Butylhydroquinone (TBHQ) is a synthetic phenolic antioxidant particularly effective in fats and oils. It is used in small amounts to slow oxidative rancidity and protect flavour or shelf life in fat-containing foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps protect fats and oils from oxidation.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority compared two exposure models for 319. A worst-case calculation that assumed foods contained the maximum permitted amount placed some high-consuming toddlers and children above the safety limit. When the authority used reported use levels and analytical results instead, no population group exceeded the limit. The revised estimate shows why maximum legal permission and likely real exposure can lead to different conclusions.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Refined exposure assessment of TBHQ E319 (2016)

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium lactate is the calcium salt of lactic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium lactate is the calcium salt of lactic acid. It keeps the familiar lactic-acid chemistry but in a less acidic salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising lactic acid — commonly produced by fermentation of sugars — with a calcium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from lactic acid, the acid associated with many fermented foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt, can regulate acidity, retain moisture, firm texture or support preservation.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium citrate is a calcium salt of citric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium citrate is a calcium salt of citric acid. It is used when food technologists want citrate chemistry with less direct acidity than citric acid itself.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising fermentation-produced citric acid with a calcium-containing base and crystallising the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from citric acid, the acid naturally associated with citrus fruit.
entries.fact_2_copy: Commonly used to regulate acidity, buffer pH or provide mineral/citrate functionality.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium phosphates are a family of sodium salts of phosphoric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium phosphates are a family of sodium salts of phosphoric acid. Schedule 8 groups several mono-, di- or tribasic forms under the same additive number.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting purified phosphoric acid with sodium-containing mineral or chemical bases and controlling the degree of neutralisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Different phosphate forms have different acidity, solubility and buffering behaviour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the form, phosphates can regulate acidity, act in raising systems, stabilise texture or bind water.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority assessed 339 with the wider phosphate group because its phosphate joins phosphorus from the rest of the diet. It found no evidence of gene damage or cancer, but the group safety value was designed for healthy people and does not cover moderate or severe kidney impairment. The sodium in 339 also counts towards dietary sodium. For someone managing kidney disease, cumulative phosphorus from food and supplements matters more than one occurrence of 339.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.tile_summary: Sodium malate / sodium hydrogen malate is a sodium salt of malic acid, the tart fruit acid associated with apples and many other fruits.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium malate / sodium hydrogen malate is a sodium salt of malic acid, the tart fruit acid associated with apples and many other fruits.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified malic acid with a sodium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from malic acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control, buffering or mineral delivery depending on the salt.

entries.tile_summary: Potassium adipate is a potassium salt of adipic acid, a manufactured dicarboxylic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium adipate is a potassium salt of adipic acid, a manufactured dicarboxylic acid.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising adipic acid with a potassium-containing base and purifying the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from adipic acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control or related processing functions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium fumarate is the ammonium salt of fumaric acid, a strong dicarboxylic food acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium fumarate is the ammonium salt of fumaric acid, a strong dicarboxylic food acid.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified fumaric acid with a ammonium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from fumaric acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control, buffering or related processing effects.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium alginate is the sodium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium alginate is the sodium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Brown seaweed is washed, extracted and processed to isolate alginate; the required acid or salt form is then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Alginate is a structural polysaccharide in brown algae.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to thicken, stabilise or form gels depending on the form and food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Carrageenan is a family of sulphated carbohydrates extracted from red seaweed.
entries.expanded_summary: Carrageenan is a family of sulphated carbohydrates extracted from red seaweed. Different carrageenan types form different textures and interact strongly with proteins such as those in milk.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Red seaweed is extracted with hot water or alkali, then the carrageenan is separated, purified, dried and milled.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from selected red algae.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to thicken, stabilise or gel foods.
entries.fact_3_label: Why one name covers several behaviours
entries.fact_3_copy: Kappa, iota and lambda carrageenan have different sulphation patterns and therefore different texture properties.
entries.evidence_copy: Public discussion often confuses food-grade carrageenan with poligeenan, but they are different materials. Poligeenan is made using harsh acid and heat treatment, has a much lower molecular weight and is not authorised as a food additive. Europe's food-safety authority found no evidence of gene damage or cancer from food-grade carrageenan. It kept the group intake limit temporary because the molecular-weight information, low-molecular-weight fractions and exposure data still needed improvement.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of carrageenan E407 and processed Eucheuma seaweed E407a (2018)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Acacia / gum arabic is a soluble gum collected from Acacia/Senegalia tree exudates.
entries.expanded_summary: Acacia / gum arabic is a soluble gum collected from Acacia/Senegalia tree exudates. It is a plant-derived hydrocolloid used to manage texture and water in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected or extracted from gum exuded from acacia-family trees, then cleaned, milled and/or purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A high-molecular-weight carbohydrate rather than a simple sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for thickening, stabilising or controlling texture.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol found naturally in some plants, mushrooms and seaweeds.
entries.expanded_summary: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol found naturally in some plants, mushrooms and seaweeds. Food-grade mannitol provides sweetness with a cooling sensation and can also act as a bulking agent.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial mannitol can be produced by hydrogenation of sugars or by fermentation, followed by crystallisation and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Occurs naturally in foods including some mushrooms and seaweeds.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a sweetener, bulking agent, anticaking aid or texture ingredient depending on the application.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Polysorbate 65 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and mostly stearic acid in a tristearate form.
entries.expanded_summary: Polysorbate 65 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and mostly stearic acid in a tristearate form. Its molecular design gives it both water-friendly and fat-friendly parts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying sorbitol/sorbitan with fatty acids and adding polyoxyethylene chains through controlled chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps oils, fats and water stay mixed and can stabilise foams or dispersions.
entries.fact_2_copy: The fatty-acid feedstock may come from plant or animal fats, while the final emulsifier is chemically processed.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Tripolyphosphates are condensed phosphate salts in which phosphate units are linked together; this Schedule 8 number covers several sodium and/or potassium forms.
entries.expanded_summary: Tripolyphosphates are condensed phosphate salts in which phosphate units are linked together; this Schedule 8 number covers several sodium and/or potassium forms. Compared with simple phosphates, their chain structure gives different water-binding, buffering and texture effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by heating and condensing purified phosphate salts under controlled conditions, then forming the required sodium or potassium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: A chain of three phosphate units.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can act in raising systems, moisture retention, emulsification, sequestration or texture control depending on the food.
entries.evidence_copy: The phosphate from 451 is absorbed efficiently and joins phosphorus from the rest of the diet. Europe's food-safety authority found no evidence of gene damage or cancer, but its group assessment showed that high total exposure could approach or exceed the safety value in younger age groups. That value did not cover people with moderate or severe kidney impairment. For those consumers, cumulative phosphorus is the important context.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Hydroxypropyl cellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose.
entries.expanded_summary: Hydroxypropyl cellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose. Introducing hydroxypropyl groups changes cellulose from an insoluble plant fibre into a material with useful thickening, film-forming or stabilising behaviour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with purified plant cellulose, which is reacted under controlled conditions to introduce hydroxypropyl groups; the product is then washed and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant cellulose, commonly from wood pulp or cotton-derived material.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a thickener, stabiliser, film former or texture modifier depending on the derivative.

entries.consumer_display_name: Acetic and fatty acid esters of glycerol
entries.entry_title: Acetic and fatty acid esters of glycerol (472a)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Acetic and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding acetic acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules.
entries.expanded_summary: Acetic and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding acetic acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules. The modification changes how the molecules interact with dough, fat and water.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made from glycerol/fatty-acid materials plus acetic acid-derived components through controlled esterification; fatty-acid sources can be plant or animal.
entries.fact_1_copy: Built on glycerol and fatty acids, the same broad building blocks found in edible fats.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as emulsifiers and texture/process aids, with some forms particularly important in bakery applications.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids are emulsifiers built from short chains of glycerol joined to fatty acids.
entries.expanded_summary: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids are emulsifiers built from short chains of glycerol joined to fatty acids. Their exact composition is a controlled mixture rather than one single molecule.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glycerol is polymerised to polyglycerol and then esterified with food fatty acids; fatty-acid sources can be plant or animal.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as emulsifiers, aeration aids and texture modifiers.
entries.fact_2_copy: A family of related esters, not one single pure compound.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. entries.tile_summary: Sorbitan monostearate is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived sorbitan and stearic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sorbitan monostearate is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived sorbitan and stearic acid. The molecule carries one stearic-acid group, which tunes how it behaves in fats and emulsions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by dehydrating sorbitol to sorbitan and esterifying it with stearic acid; the fatty-acid starting material can come from plant or animal fats.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to emulsify and stabilise fat-containing foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: The final ingredient is manufactured even though its fatty-acid feedstock may originate from edible fats or oils.

entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a carrier, acidity-related processing aid or firming/standardising material in specified uses.

entries.expanded_summary: Potassium hydroxide, also known as caustic potash, is an inorganic alkaline material. It is strongly alkaline and is used for pH adjustment, processing and some cocoa/food treatments.

entries.fact_1_copy: A strongly or moderately basic potassium-containing compound used for processing rather than flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its technical name can sound severe because concentrated material is reactive; food use is controlled and application-specific.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium aluminium phosphate is a family of inorganic phosphate salts containing sodium and aluminium.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium aluminium phosphate is a family of inorganic phosphate salts containing sodium and aluminium. Different acidic or basic forms are used for leavening and other processing effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled reaction of aluminium, sodium and phosphate raw materials to produce defined food-grade phosphate salts.
entries.fact_1_copy: Some forms act as acid components in baking powders, releasing carbon dioxide when paired with bicarbonate.
entries.fact_2_copy: This is a mineral phosphate salt, not metallic aluminium.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium aluminium silicate is a mica-like potassium aluminosilicate.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium aluminium silicate is a mica-like potassium aluminosilicate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from purified mineral mica or produced/processed to defined specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a carrier or pearlescent/mineral substrate in specified applications.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Glucono delta-lactone (575) gradually turns into an acid in water, allowing acidity to develop over time.
entries.expanded_summary: Glucono delta-lactone (575) is a cyclic form of gluconic acid made from glucose. In water, it gradually converts to gluconic acid, allowing acidity to develop over time. This makes it useful for controlled acidification and certain food-setting processes.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glucose is oxidised — commonly by microbial fermentation — to gluconic acid, which is then concentrated and converted to the lactone form.
entries.fact_1_copy: It slowly releases acidity as the lactone opens to gluconic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for controlled acidification, leavening, curing, coagulation and pH control.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: 4-Hexylresorcinol is a synthetic phenolic compound used in a narrow range of foods for antioxidant and anti-browning effects.
entries.expanded_summary: 4-Hexylresorcinol is a synthetic phenolic compound used in a narrow range of foods for antioxidant and anti-browning effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis and purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used particularly to help prevent enzymatic browning in some seafood products.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Magnesium glutamate is the magnesium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste.
entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium glutamate is the magnesium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste. It belongs to the same glutamate flavour-enhancer family as MSG.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glutamic acid is commonly produced by microbial fermentation of sugars or starch hydrolysates, then neutralised with a magnesium source to make the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glutamate occurs naturally in foods including tomatoes, mushrooms, seaweed and aged cheeses.
entries.fact_2_copy: The glutamate ion provides savoury umami taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Added glutamate and naturally occurring glutamate are the same glutamate ion once dissolved in food.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Glycine is the smallest amino acid and is a normal building block of proteins in foods and the human body.
entries.expanded_summary: Glycine is the smallest amino acid and is a normal building block of proteins in foods and the human body. As an additive it can contribute mild sweetness, buffering or processing effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial glycine is produced by chemical synthesis or fermentation, then crystallised and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Present in proteins throughout ordinary foods and the body.
entries.fact_2_copy: Glycine has a mildly sweet taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used for flavour, buffering or other technological purposes depending on the product.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with material from crude-oil refining, then undergoes extensive refining and purification to meet food-grade specifications. The petroleum origin remains factual even though the finished material is highly purified.
entries.tile_summary: Petrolatum, or petroleum jelly, is a highly refined semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons derived from petroleum.
entries.expanded_summary: Petrolatum, or petroleum jelly, is a highly refined semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons derived from petroleum. Food-grade material is purified to much tighter specifications than crude petroleum products.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by refining and purifying selected petroleum fractions to remove unwanted components and create a stable semi-solid hydrocarbon mixture.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for surface coating, release or glazing functions in specified applications.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Isobutane is a branched isomer of butane.
entries.expanded_summary: Isobutane is a branched isomer of butane.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Separated or manufactured from hydrocarbon processing streams and purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a propellant in specified food applications.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Saccharin is one of the oldest high-intensity synthetic sweeteners.
entries.expanded_summary: Saccharin is one of the oldest high-intensity synthetic sweeteners. It is much sweeter than sugar and is used in very small amounts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis; food products may use saccharin itself or approved soluble salts depending on the formulation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Several hundred times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to provide intense sweetness with negligible bulk.
entries.fact_3_copy: Saccharin has been used as a sweetener since the late 19th century.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Aspartame-acesulphame salt is a crystalline compound containing the two sweeteners aspartame and acesulphame in a fixed salt-like combination.
entries.expanded_summary: Aspartame-acesulphame salt is a crystalline compound containing the two sweeteners aspartame and acesulphame in a fixed salt-like combination.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by combining purified aspartame and acesulphame components under controlled conditions and crystallising the resulting compound.
entries.fact_1_copy: Two established high-intensity sweetener components in one ingredient.
entries.fact_2_copy: Provides a blended sweetness profile without adding the two sweeteners separately.
entries.fact_3_copy: The ingredient contains aspartame-derived material as well as acesulphame.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Choline salts are forms of choline, an essential nutrient-like compound used by the body to make cell membranes and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine.
entries.expanded_summary: Choline salts are forms of choline, an essential nutrient-like compound used by the body to make cell membranes and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Different salt forms are used to make choline stable and practical in formulations.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial choline salts are manufactured from purified chemical starting materials and crystallised or formulated in stable salt forms.
entries.fact_1_copy: Choline is a normal component of human metabolism and phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the product, choline salts may serve nutritional or technological formulation purposes.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive entry can cover more than one choline salt form.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Polydextrose is a highly branched glucose polymer used as a low-sweetness bulking ingredient and soluble fibre-like material.
entries.expanded_summary: Polydextrose is a highly branched glucose polymer used as a low-sweetness bulking ingredient and soluble fibre-like material. It is designed to replace some of the bulk normally provided by sugar or fat.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by heating glucose with small amounts of sorbitol and an acid catalyst, producing a randomly bonded polymer that is then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Mostly glucose, but the final structure is very different from ordinary starch or sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for bulking, texture, moisture control and fibre enrichment.
entries.fact_3_copy: Its irregular bonds are only partly digested in the small intestine.
entries.evidence_copy: A United Nations food-additive expert committee did not consider a numerical toxicological limit necessary for the assessed uses of polydextrose. This does not mean unlimited use. Larger amounts can still have an immediate digestive effect, which is why relevant Australia and New Zealand foods must state that excess consumption may have a laxative effect. The statement prompts consumers to consider serving size and other polyols in the same product; it is not a warning about long-term poisoning.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: Warning and advisory statements (updated 2025-11-26)
entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: United Nations food-additive expert committee: Polydextroses INS 1200 evaluation (1987)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Oxidised starch is starch deliberately oxidised to introduce carbonyl/carboxyl groups and reduce chain length.
entries.expanded_summary: Oxidised starch is starch deliberately oxidised to introduce carbonyl/carboxyl groups and reduce chain length. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes controlled oxidation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Starch acetate is starch carrying acetyl groups.
entries.expanded_summary: Starch acetate is starch carrying acetyl groups. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes acetylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Triethyl citrate is the triethyl ester of citric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Triethyl citrate is the triethyl ester of citric acid. It is a clear, mildly oily liquid used as a solvent, carrier and plasticising ingredient in specialised food applications.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by esterifying citric acid with ethanol and purifying the resulting triester.
entries.fact_1_copy: Citric acid plus ethanol.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a carrier/solvent, flavour-related processing ingredient or coating plasticiser depending on the application.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Quillaia extract type 2 is a more highly purified saponin-rich extract made from the bark or wood of the soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria.
entries.expanded_summary: Quillaia extract type 2 is a more highly purified saponin-rich extract made from the bark or wood of the soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria. Its key components are saponins — plant molecules that can stabilise foam and emulsions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by water extraction of soapbark tree material, followed by filtration and concentration; type 2 undergoes more extensive purification than type 1.
entries.fact_1_copy: Quillaja saponaria, a South American tree also called soapbark.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a foaming agent and emulsifier, especially in beverages.
entries.fact_3_copy: The types differ mainly in purification and composition, not in the basic plant source.
